articles.title: So you want to buy AI for your company
articles.summary:
Where do I start?
We have Gemini 4 Hydrogen. But it sounds like you could use Claude Sonnet 5.5. Or maybe 5.4; it really depends. Have you tried Opus? We have Opus 5.2 right now. It's similar to Fable 5.2, but better for day-to-day work. It's not quite as powerful as Mythos 5.2, though. I hear the gap will narrow eventually. Opus scores 94.8 on a benchmark, while Mythos gets 96.1. Fable is a respectable 92.7, assuming you don't ask it to do anything too ambitious.
Have you tried the Chinese models? DeepSeek is pretty good. You might want to start with the R1 family to test the waters before moving on to V4. Personally, I'm a Flash kind of guy, but Pro is pretty good too. The crowd favorite is GLM these days. You've got to try 5.3 Flash. Its Mixture-of-Experts architecture is state of the art, in my opinion. It scores an impressive 87.3 on the Benchmark Performance Index.
But let's be serious for a minute. You're probably looking for ChatGPT. Astra is overkill unless you want to do some damage. I'd stick with GPT-6.0 Terra, not Sol! That one ate through my budget in three days. Terra gets 98.2 on the Enterprise Productivity Benchmark, while Sol gets 99.1. That extra 0.9 will cost you $14,000 a month. So go with Luna if you must.
If you're feeling more adventurous, you could go with Qwen, though. I'd stick with 3.8 MoE. Don't even think about 4 Plus. It's a nightmare. Kimi K is dear to my heart, though. You can't go wrong with it. I use it alongside Codex to complement my workflow. Really great. It scored 91.6 on SWE.
Those are just some of the options.
If you're a programmer, you probably don't need any of that. You just want to use Claude Code. Or get Cursor. Make sure to remove Grok from the auto-selection options. You don't want Grok. If you don't know why, then you don't need to know why.
Anyway, I use Jules with Antigravity now. In VS Code, I use Continue with a local R1 Flash running on Ollama. I use Qwen3.5-397B-A17B for setting up machines, and Qwen-VL to read through my camera feeds. The latter is particularly good at detecting forklifts.
And that's pretty much it. A fairly simple setup, really.
For the layperson, though, it's much easier: they just use the free ChatGPT tier and call it a day... Or Argon. It depends really. Google 3.6 Flash has the lowest score, but it is great for email. I mean how mean do you need your email game to be? Anyway, that's it.
Nano Banana! You probably need that too. It's great with Omni or Carbon. Or wait next week when Hydrocarbon comes out.
That's it!

Hi HN! Showcasing this fun project. I took 1300 square miles of the SF Bay Area from Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles and transformed them into a cohesive pixel map. It's really fun to explore and stumble upon various famous landmarks like Apple Park, Palace of Fine Arts, or UC Berkeley.

articles.title: NYT: ‘Howard Lutnick Took Softer Line on Nvidia as Calls for Tougher Controls Grew’
articles.summary:
Ana Swanson, Tripp Mickle, Maggie Haberman, and Jonathan Swan, in a long deeply-sourced profile of Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick (gift link):
There is broad agreement among most senior Trump administration
officials that the United States should more aggressively tighten
controls on Nvidia’s advanced chips to keep China from using them
to catch up in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.
Then there is Howard Lutnick, who runs the Commerce
Department. [...]
Within the Commerce Department, Nvidia is treated differently than
other firms, current and former officials say, with its issues
given high priority and sent through specific channels.
Mr. Lutnick frequently calls and messages with Mr. Huang, and the
department prepares carefully for their private meetings together
in Mr. Lutnick’s fifth floor office. All Nvidia matters are routed
through Jeff Kessler, a top deputy to Mr. Lutnick, who is said to
rarely take any significant action without the commerce
secretary’s approval.
Nvidia’s general counsel has also been given direct access to
shape new rules, including leaving comments in draft regulations
affecting the company.
Here’s a photo from the Times story, taken this July in the Washington D.C. Cheesecake Factory, with Lutnick telling Jensen Huang, “Dude, seriously, smell my finger...”

Republicans as a party, and the Trump administration in particular, need scapegoats for the historical disaster of their election losses last week. Huang and Nvidia are going to be one of them. Lutnick is another. He’s cooked.
 ★

articles.title: Andrew Sharp: ‘Jensen Huang Was Always Going to Lose’
articles.summary:
Andrew Sharp, in an excellent column at Sharp Text:
I have a variety of thoughts after spending the past several days
reading and recording podcasts about these (figurative and
literal) affairs, but let me express one unpopular sentiment at
the outset: what happened to Jensen Huang this week is tragic and
depressing.
I have a disease that makes me sympathetic to almost anyone who
ends up on the wrong end of viral outrage and panic, and
unfortunately it’s flaring up again. Huang is one of the greatest
CEOs in American history. He’s still hyper competent, he’s been
incredibly important to the growth of the AI ecosystem, and
frankly, he’s among the most sane of the contemporary tech leaders
we have on offer. His fall from grace has been not only stunning
but seemingly coordinated.
It is sad. But it’s also funny. Many tragedies are also hilarious. (That’s a key to Shakespeare’s enduring fame — his tragedies had funny scenes and his comedies had painful themes.)
But I think it’s now a very open question whether Jensen Huang was even a vaguely responsible CEO, let alone “one of the greatest CEOs in American history”. What’s undisputed is that he’s one of the greatest technical innovators in history. Nvidia technology is world-beating in several regards. But that doesn’t make him a great CEO. If Nvidia falls apart because he — by his own admission — rejected the notion of succession planning and structured the company with no hierarchy other than himself at the center, that’s an abject failure. Ignoring the fact that he himself knew the risks he was taking with his sexual escapades, he could have been hit by a bus on any given day. The leadership structure Huang cultivated is like being the sole breadwinner in a family and not having a life insurance policy. If that breadwinner dies in an accident and leaves their family destitute, no one’s going to call them “one of the greatest parents in history”. Maybe it’ll all work out for Nvidia though. We don’t know yet. Only time will tell. But I don’t think it looks good at the moment. If I owned Nvidia stock I’d sell it all right now.
The above doesn’t even touch upon my belief that Nvidia’s meteoric rise to the top market cap in the world was fueled — to some extent — by a circular financing racket. If my side of that argument is ultimately proven correct — that the AI bubble is essentially an elaborate, complex Ponzi scheme — Huang’s plaque in the CEO Hall of Fame will go in the Infamy Wing alongside Enron’s Jeffrey Skilling, Elizabeth Holmes, and     Sam Bankman-Fried. Maybe I’m all wet about that. But I’d say it’s at least an open question at the moment.
Sharp, nearing his conclusion:
Huang repeatedly belittled those people with both his rhetoric and
his company’s behavior, and indeed, he questioned the patriotism
of anyone who dared to object. In so doing, he was waging war with
not only large swaths of the U.S. security apparatus, but also the
realities of Xi Jinping’s China that would inevitably make it
impossible to sustain his position without looking naive, selfish,
and unforgivably reckless.
Read the whole thing, and Sharp ends up making the case himself that Huang, ultimately, was a terrible CEO, not a great one.
 ★

articles.title: Pluralistic: I told you so (13 Nov 2026)
articles.summary: Today's links I told you so: Microsoft is too big to live. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Canada's corrupt copyright czar; Universal Music CEO v iPod owners; Berlusconi x neo-fascists; Balancing 3,118 coins on a dime; All for-profit healthcare is a problem. Upcoming appearances: Folkestone, Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. I told you so (permalink) Here's the one weird trick that made it possible for monopolies to conquer the world: the antitrust bar changed the rules so that it was impossible to prove whether a company had formed an illegal monopoly, and then these rules meant that monopolies were almost never challenged, and what challenges did arise were usually unsuccessful, and even the successful challenges resulted in meaningless "penalties" that left monopolists unscathed. Every policy has three important dimensions: substance, scope and administrability: "Substance" is what the policy actually says. For example, the basic substance of copyright law is, "You can't display, transmit or reproduce a copyrighted work without permission." "Scope" is when the policy gets applied. When copyright law was formulated, the key activities it regulated all required a bunch of expensive industrial equipment. Every book implied a printing press, every record implied a record-pressing plant, every film implied a film duplication lab. That meant that, by default, pretty much the only people who had to care about what copyright law said were industrial actors – firms who might reasonably be expected to also have access to a lawyer. That matters a lot to administrability. "Administrability" is what it takes to actually administer the policy. Can you detect potential violations, and when you do, how hard is it to figure out whether the rule was actually broken? Again, in the pre-digital era, it was pretty easy to spot copyright violations: pirate books, records and movies are tangible, physical objects, and distributing them requires advertisement, delivery and payment. After detecting an infringement, copyright enforcers must resolve a further question: whether a display, transmission or copy fall under "fair use." Fair use is a "fact intensive" rule, one that requires a lot of evidence and argument to adjudicate. It's almost impossible to categorically rule in or rule out a specific use as "fair": https://pluralistic.net/2024/06/27/nuke-first/#ask-questions-never Despite the complexity and expense of determining fair use, pre-digital copyright was still relatively administrable, because fair use questions themselves were relatively rare. Most fair uses (for example, photocopying part of a book for classroom use) were below the threshold for detection by rightsholders, so these questions almost never found their way into court. The fair use questions that did get to court were big, splashy affairs, like whether it's okay to rewrite a famous pro-slavery novel from the enslaved characters' perspective (it is!): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wind_Done_Gone There are a lot of legal questions that require nuance, fact-finding and argumentation to resolve, and that's not necessarily a problem. It's fine to apply these complicated, lengthy processes to things that only happen every once in a while. Take probate: most of us will die one or fewer times, so it's not the worst thing in the world that figuring out what happens to our stuff when that happens can involve some legal complexity. But as media went digital, copyright's scope expanded dramatically. "Making or handling copies of copyrighted work" stopped being an industrial activity that implied a complex business and access to legal expertise. The only thing a digital computer does is make and handle copies, so every time any ordinary person clicks their mouse, dozens of potentially thorny copyright questions arise. What's more, those questions involve the public internet, which raises the number of potential infringements that a rightsholder can detect (and potentially seek legal redress for) from dozens to millions. Nearly all of these potential infringements fall under fair use, but fair use is a fact-intensive doctrine suited to resolving occasional disputes between large firms. Fair use is monumentally unsuited to resolving questions that arise hundreds of times every day for nearly every person alive, including small children and other people who almost certainly can't get legal advice: https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-a-new-deal-for-copyright/ This is how copyright broke: new technology (digital computers) radically expanded its scope, conscripting everyone into using copyright's framework for everyday activities that had nothing to do with the media industry's supply-chain. That framework was developed for industrial actors with access to lawyers, and its most important aspect (fair use) is a fact-intensive doctrine that takes serious work to resolve, but now had to be navigated many times every day by every person. So copyright became unadministrable: you can't apply a fact-intensive doctrine to everyday activities undertaken by everyday people. If you try, you will make criminals of everyone. It would be literally impossible to train enough copyright lawyers to advise every person every time they use a computer to do something that might violate copyright law. Back to antitrust: when the pro-monopoly partisans of the "law and economy" movement set out to neuter antitrust, they deliberately introduced a set of hurdles that were designed to make it impossible to administer competition law. First, they introduced an "intent" standard: it was no longer enough for a company to have a monopoly, the company must have intended to secure and maintain that monopoly. If you want to be sure a law doesn't get enforced, this is a fantastic standard to apply. After all, how can anyone know what anyone else intended? Ask any anthropologist and they'll tell you: the only way to find out what someone intends by their actions is to ask them, and even that only works if you can trust them to answer honestly: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thick_description#Clifford_Geertz If antitrust law can only be enforced by mind-readers and advanced philosophers who have solved the intersubjectivity problem, then antitrust law can't be enforced at all: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intersubjective_verifiability But that wasn't all! Antitrust's enemies insisted on another fact-intensive question: "market definition." They made the (seemingly commonsense) point that if a company is said to have a monopoly, we must first determine which thing the company has monopolized. This sounds like a no-brainer, but it's actually a way to introduce unresolvable, show-stopper arguments into any antitrust enforcement action. Take Amazon: the company's ecommerce monopoly is obvious to anyone who hasn't been in a coma for the past 15 years. But when Amazon gets investigated for this monopoly, they will insist that they don't participate in the "ecommerce" economy, but rather in "the buying and selling of things in general." Then they point out that people still go to the corner store for a pint of milk, still buy a pack of gum from the kiosk at the train-station, and still buy some hair-gel from the barber after a trim, and therefore Amazon can't possibly have a monopoly. "Market definition" is a playground for bad-faith semanticians. Luckily for the world's monopolists, the very existence of this legal doctrine has conjured up an army of bad-faith semanticians, most of them with expensive Ivy League economics degrees, who make millions coming up with bizarre market definition arguments that can draw out any legal proceeding for years, often to the point where there is a change in government and the federal prosecutors just walk away from the case. Taken together, these impossible fact-intensive questions would be enough to bury antitrust, but then came the final blow: frequency. Once capital had won the battle to mire antitrust cases in questions that take years and millions to resolve, they embarked on a frenzy of monopolistic mergers. This meant that the kind of antitrust questions that originally arose every few years were suddenly coming up several times per month. This was the killer combo: making antitrust a plodding ball-ache of thorny philosophical and technical questions, and then rigging the system so that these questions arise in a nonstop flurry guaranteed that antitrust would fail. That's what happened with Microsoft. The company had a 95% desktop OS market-share when Clinton's trustbusters dragged them into court. Nevertheless, the company played all kinds of "market definition" games that dragged the case out for years. They also insisted that they never intended to form a monopoly, despite smoking-gun memos about "sucking up all the market oxygen": https://web.archive.org/web/20190717023522/https://www.justice.gov/atr/department-justice-7 This dragged on so long that even after Microsoft lost its case, the appeal carried on until after GW Bush stole the presidency, and then his DoJ walked away from the case, letting Microsoft continue to enjoy (and increase) its monopoly: https://www.nytimes.com/2001/09/07/business/us-vs-microsoft-overview-us-abandoning-its-effort-break-apart-microsoft-saying.html What happened next should not come as a surprise to anyone. Microsoft got convicted of deliberately setting out to create a monopoly, and then paid no penalty. After an all-too-brief period of post-traumatic good behavior, Microsoft returned to its monopolistic ways. Along the way, Microsoft sucked up to a succession of presidential administrations, culminating in the company's emergence as a de facto wing of the Trump regime. Microsoft's CEO paid $1m to sit on the inaugural dais, and then directed the company to donate millions to the Epstein Ballroom, and then provided the IT services for ICE's ethnic cleansing pogroms: https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/us-ice-triples-use-of-microsoft-cloud-in-six-months/#:~:text=ICE%20has%20been,first%20presidential%20term. Microsoft isn't merely the in-house IT shop for Trump's domestic agenda: they've also weaponized foreign reliance on Microsoft's cloud apps and they punish foreign officials who thwart Trump abroad: https://www.theregister.com/off-prem/2026/02/18/microsoft-throws-spox-under-the-bus-in-icc-email-flap/ When forced, Microsoft candidly admits that no matter where in the world your Microsoft data is stored, when it comes to foreign firms and governments, the company will give warrantless, secret access to their data to Trump's cronies: https://www.theregister.com/off-prem/2025/07/25/microsoft-exec-admits-it-cannot-guarantee-data-sovereignty/458553 All of this raises an urgent digital sovereignty question: what if Microsoft (a monopolist that is entirely dependent on Trump's favor to keep it free of existential legal problems) cuts off your country's Office 365 access? This is the question I raised late last year in my CCC talk about the "Post-American Internet": https://pluralistic.net/2026/01/01/39c3/#the-new-coalition (Coming soon in expanded form to a bookstore near you:) https://us.macmillan.com/books/9780374623845/thepostamericaninternet/ And now, Microsoft has given the whole world a preview of how this might play out, because their servers have collapsed, shutting the world off from Outlook email, Azure cloud, Copilot, Teams, and other key offerings: https://www.bbc.com/news/live/cq5y10ge3dp3t The outage lasted for about two days, and around the world, government agencies and businesses large and small ground to a halt. Without Office 365, Outlook and Teams, many organizations could not even convene a meeting or formulate a plan to deal with the outage. All of this raises an important question: is Microsoft guilty of negligence, and, if so, what should be done about this? Here's my answer: yes, Microsoft is presumptively guilty of negligence, and any response to this must include antitrust breakups of the company. Here's why I think that. Microsoft has demonstrably underinvested in its IT stability. Any IT plan that results in a global, multi-day outage is, by definition, inadequate. Whether the problem could have been solved by buying more servers, or hiring more people, or changing the management of key divisions is immaterial. Every one of these measures – every single measure that could have prevented this – costs money. By not spending that money, Microsoft definitively underinvested in its products. But Microsoft doesn't lack for funds! Microsoft is a convicted monopolist, and it has the margins to prove it. In 2025-2026, the company pissed away more than $30b in stock buybacks, a once-illegal (and still sleazy) form of stock manipulation. Over that same period, Microsoft lost nearly $200b on AI ventures that it now admits will not pay off: https://www.cnbc.com/2025/02/24/microsoft-reiterates-plan-to-invest-80-billion-in-ai-.html Then there's the layoffs. 2026 saw Microsoft's first-ever voluntary retirement buyout, which served as the overture to a year that saw a 25% headcount cut – 60,000 employees slated for destruction: https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/oct/26/microsoft-buyout-offers-ai-cuts Ever had a boss who caught you catching your breath and shoved a broom in your hand, barking, "If you have time to lean, you have time to clean?" That goes quintuple for convicted monopolists who bring the global economy to a halt due to a multi-day outage. If you can't manage to keep your servers online, you have no business incinerating tens of billions on stock buybacks, much less hundreds of billions to feed the AI money-furnace. Did Microsoft need the tens of thousands of workers it threw away? Demonstrably so: when they were on the payroll, Microsoft's servers were up. Now they're gone, and so are the servers. It doesn't matter how those workers related to this specific outage: if you can't keep your servers online, you either don't have enough site reliability engineers, or you don't have enough managers to deploy them effectively, or you don't have enough managers to hire the managers and SREs you need. Q.E.D. This is all characteristic of the monopolist's pathology. The problem with monopolists is that they have pricing power and market power: the power to foist inferior products on their customers and degraded working conditions on their employees and unfair terms on their suppliers. Microsoft's hundreds of billions in wastage and tens of thousands of layoffs are a massive transfer of value from customers, workers and suppliers to investors. The fact that the company judged (correctly, it seems) that they could make us all eat shit and we'd ask for second helpings is a nice, clean proof of monopoly power. Here, I think, is a nice, bright-line, administrable test for monopoly power. If your company has a dominant position and if it allocates its surplus capital to its investors and if that precedes a significant degradation of your products, then you have an illegal monopoly and you should be broken up. We don't need to inquire as to whether you have a wicked heart that intentionally set about to create a monopoly, nor do we have to argue endlessly about how many angels can dance on the head of your market definition. If you think you are so powerful that you can fuck up your products and not suffer as a result then you are too big to care, and that is simply too big. This isn't the only fix we need to antitrust law, but it is a fix that would specifically let us target Big Tech. Microsoft is a living, breathing (limping, gasping) repudiation of the thesis that monopolies are efficient and if we only let them amass endless market share and profits, they will use their "economies of scale" to deliver superior products. It's not that economies of scale don't exist, but for companies to take advantage of these economies of scale, they have to be motivated to expend their capital to do so. The more powerful a company is, the less inclined it will be to apportion capital to workers, suppliers and consumers, and the more it will cheat us all to enrich its shareholders. We can't afford to let this crisis go to waste. Google was convicted of creating and maintaining a monopoly three times over the past couple years and every single time the judge decided the company should not face any real punishment for that monopoly, on the basis that the monopoly is what lets Google deliver such excellence for us. Does anyone still think Google is excellent? How about Apple? Google pays Apple an annual bribe of more than $20b to stay out of the search market. Judge Amit Mehta decided to let Google continue paying this bribe to Apple so that Apple would have the capital it needed to deliver excellent products. Apple promptly went on to have a string of catastrophically bad product launches – while throwing away $170b manipulating its share-price with stock buybacks: https://finance.yahoo.com/news/apple-dodged-a-20-billion-hit-thanks-to-google-antitrust-ruling-163056806.html Both companies are demonstrably underinvesting in quality in order to divert R&D and product maintenance capital to their shareholders. They are too big to care. In this age of nonstop mergers and acquisitions, we can't afford to make merger approval turn on fact-intensive questions, but we can sure as hell create this administrable, bright-line test for whether a merger should be unwound after the fact. Did your company buy another company and then enshittify both products? Great, now we're breaking you up, and your investors are getting fucked. Maybe next time they'll fire the board when they announce another stupid, anti-competitive merger. Microsoft is too big in every way. Too big to fail, too big to jail and too big to care. Too big to trust. Too big to rely upon. Too big to foster a corporate culture that cares about reliability, a decent workplace, or product quality. There's a straight line from GW Bush's decision to let Microsoft skate in 2001 and the situation a quarter century later, where Microsoft is a load-bearing piece of the world's most important firms and government agencies, and where this means that Microsoft knows that it can throw away tens of thousands of workers and hundreds of billions of dollars, crash the planet, and wake up tomorrow unscathed, ready to do it all over again. articles.summary:
David Sacks, on X:
Bombshell story. The spy narrative is collapsing already.
Is there clear & convincing evidence that Alice Huang was a
Chinese spy?
AG says no. (“no conclusions reached”).
CIA says no. (“not yet convinced”).
DNI says no (“not entirely accurate and over-torqued”).
Ranking Democrat on House Intelligence (incoming Chairman) says
no. (“today, at least, I don’t know”). This was immediately
after he was briefed.
Who argues otherwise? Anonymous officials tell CNN “it strains
credulity to believe that she was not acting as an agent of the
Chinese government — simply by virtue of the fact that she is a
successful Chinese businesswoman working with one of America’s
most powerful companies.”
First, as for “who argues otherwise?”, the U.S. State Department is who. But more importantly, the degree to which Alice Huang worked for or with China’s MSS is almost a footnote on this scandal. It’s not central to the story at all.
It’s bad enough that Jensen Huang was having a yearslong affair with an executive from any Nvidia client. But Megaspeed was apparently a shell company dedicated to circumventing U.S. export controls for AI hardware to China. Alice Huang is, apparently, a criminal smuggler working to circumvent U.S. national security policy. If she was also cooperating with or taking direction from MSS that’s just icing on the cake.
I wrote in a post earlier today that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is being teed up to be scapegoated — deservedly — for the ails of the Republican Party and Trump administration. Sacks, I think, is going to be right there with him — also deservedly. This whole “Maybe she’s not a spy so the whole story is a scam” argument is drenched with flop sweat.
Sacks originally joined Team Trump 2.0 as “AI czar”. In that capacity he was the leading proponent in the Trump administration for a hands-off approach to AI regulation generally, and specifically a look-the-other-way policy regarding Nvidia’s 20-percent-of-revenue side hustle selling banned-for-sale-to-China hardware to smugglers.
Sacks might not just get sacked. If this goes south and people wind up being convicted of crimes, Sacks will be at the front of that line too. The pardon from Trump will cost Sacks real money.
 ★

articles.title: Nvidia Employees Petition for Jensen Huang’s Return
articles.summary:
Paresh Dave and Zoë Schiffer, reporting for Wired:
Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang’s return
even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and
abrupt resignation, according to internal correspondence
reviewed by Wired.
An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s
resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s
board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to
taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600
comments since then, with several asking board members to find a
way to bring back Huang.
“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one
anonymous commenter.
Nvidia has over 42,000 employees (for now). The 1,600 who commented on this petition might just be the ones Huang was shtupping.
